body.text: Under subsection 127(8) of the Income Tax Act, investment tax credits on a partnership's SR&ED expenditures are calculated at the 15% basic rate at the partnership level and allocated to partners who are not specified members. A CCPC partner cannot claim the 35% enhanced rate, and its allocated credit is 40% refundable only if it is a qualifying corporation.

Canada’s Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and technological innovation in the country, providing close to $3 billion in tax credits annually to approximately 16,000 businesses across roughly 20,000 corporate (T2) and 4,500 individual (T1) claims filed each year1. Governed federally by Section 37, Section 127, Section 127.1, and Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) alongside Part XXIX (Regulations 2900 to 2903) and Part XLVI (Regulation 4600) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945), the program operates through a dual-incentive statutory structure3. First, taxpayers carrying on business in Canada may pool and deduct 100% of allowable current—and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, eligible capital—SR&ED expenditures against business income in the taxation year incurred or carry those undeducted pool balances forward indefinitely under Subsection 37(1)8. Second, claimants earn a federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under Subsection 127(5) and Subsection 127(9) ranging from a 15% basic rate to an enhanced 35% refundable rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures, complemented by provincial and territorial R&D tax credits in nine provinces and Yukon10.

Between December 2024 and 2026, the Canadian R&D tax framework underwent its most substantial legislative and administrative overhaul since the 2012 federal budget reforms. Enacted through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, and effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the federal government doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million (raising the maximum annual refundable enhanced federal credit from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, introduced an alternative 3-year average gross revenue phase-out test ($15 million–$75 million), extended the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs (including Shared-Use Equipment [SUE]) incurred after December 15, 20244. Concurrently, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) introduced an elective Pre-Claim Approval process supported by a 90-calendar-day expenditure review standard and artificial-intelligence risk screening12. At the provincial level, Québec eliminated seven legacy R&D tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the consolidated, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) providing 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital expenditures above an exclusion threshold and 20% thereafter, while British Columbia and Saskatchewan enacted major provincial SR&ED expansions15.

body.text: Section 1: Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to all federal, provincial, and territorial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (ITA)4. Unlike the financial provisions in Sections 37 and 127 that govern how expenditures are pooled and how tax credits are calculated once technical eligibility is established, Subsection 248(1) defines the substantive scientific and technological criteria that work must satisfy to qualify4. Under Subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of three primary categories of research and development, accompanied by eligible support work and bounded by seven explicit statutory exclusions23:

items: Basic Research — Paragraph 248(1)(a): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view15.
Applied Research — Paragraph 248(1)(b): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view15.

Experimental Development — Paragraph 248(1)(c): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto15. Paragraph 248(1)(c) deliberately encompasses incremental technological improvements rather than requiring pioneering breakthroughs, provided the work seeks to advance the underlying technological knowledge base rather than merely applying routine engineering or standard practice3.

Eligible Support Work — Paragraph 248(1)(d): Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only eight enumerated disciplines—namely (i) engineering, (ii) design, (iii) operations research, (iv) mathematical analysis, (v) computer programming, (vi) data collection, (vii) testing, or (viii) psychological research—where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer23. Work outside these eight categories (such as clerical administration or general management) cannot qualify as support work under Paragraph 248(1)(d), even if it aids an R&D project3.

Statutory Exclusions ("Excluded Work") — Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k): Subsection 248(1) expressly excludes from SR&ED any work with respect to: Paragraph (e) market research or sales promotion (work that supplements advertising, personal selling, or stimulating sales)23; Paragraph (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes23; Paragraph (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities23; Paragraph (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas23; Paragraph (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process23; Paragraph (j) style changes (iterating a product’s aesthetic form, finish, or proportions without resolving a technological uncertainty)3; or Paragraph (k) routine data collection (unless the data collection is performed specifically and commensurate with the needs to directly support basic research, applied research, or experimental development under Paragraph 248(1)(d))4.

body.text: 1.2 The CRA Two-Step Eligibility Methodology ("Why" and "How") and the Five-Question Framework

To operationalize Subsection 248(1) during technical reviews, the Canada Revenue Agency applies the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives (published August 13, 2021, replacing the 2012/2015 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy)23. The CRA’s administrative methodology—which directly reflects the judicial criteria established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada—evaluates eligibility through a Two-Step Methodology anchored in why the work was conducted and how it was carried out7.
In Step 1 (Determine Whether SR&ED Exists), the CRA and the courts examine the technical facts against five cumulative questions25:

items: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty (The "Why" — Impetus): Was there a scientific or technological uncertainty that could not be resolved on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge, standard practice, or routine engineering?3. The CRA defines the scientific or technological knowledge base as the combined knowledge of the internal resources within the business plus all sources reasonably available publicly3. Acquiring existing knowledge through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring external consultants, or purchasing proprietary off-the-shelf know-how does not satisfy the requirement of attempting to resolve a technological uncertainty23. Indicators of genuine technological uncertainty include system constraints where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications outside normal operating ranges, or complex interactions among variables that are unpredictable under established engineering principles23.

Formulation of Hypotheses (The "How" — Starting Point): Did the effort involve formulating a specific idea or hypothesis—expressed as a proposed causal relationship, method, or technical design—aimed directly at reducing or eliminating the identified scientific or technological uncertainty?23.

Systematic Investigation or Search (The "How" — Execution): Was the overall approach adopted consistent with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and testing of the hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, leading to logical conclusions and iterative modification of the hypothesis?7.

Scientific or Technological Advancement (The "Why" — Targeted Outcome): Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or technological advancement—that is, generating new knowledge that advances the company's and industry's understanding of the underlying science or technology?23. Crucially, commercial or technical failure does not disqualify a project: if a systematic experiment demonstrates that a hypothesized technological pathway cannot function under specific parameters, that negative finding still constitutes a valid technological advancement because it eliminates an uncertainty and advances the technological knowledge base26.

Contemporaneous Record Keeping (The "How" — Evidence): Was a detailed record of the hypotheses formulated, the experiments or analyses performed, and the results and conclusions kept as the work progressed?23.

body.text: In Step 2 (Determine the Extent of Eligible Work), once Step 1 establishes that a core basic research, applied research, or experimental development investigation exists, the claimant and reviewer delineate the boundaries of the SR&ED project25. Under CRA policy, an SR&ED project comprises the set of interrelated activities collectively necessary to attempt to resolve the scientific or technological uncertainty26. Activities within the eight categories of Paragraph 248(1)(d) (engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research) are included to the extent their primary purpose was to directly support the core SR&ED investigation and their scale was commensurate with the needs of that investigation23. Conversely, activities falling within Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) must be carved out3. A project’s eligible completion date is reached at the earliest of: (a) achieving the technological advancement by resolving the uncertainty, (b) determining that the uncertainty cannot be resolved, or (c) terminating the project for any reason26.
1.3 Section 37 of the Income Tax Act: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Section 37 of the Income Tax Act establishes a dedicated tax accounting mechanism known as the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures, audited under the CRA’s Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy (updated March 30, 2022 and March 27, 2026)9. Under general income tax principles, outlays that create an enduring benefit or capital asset cannot be deducted as current business expenses. Section 37 overrides general capital-versus-current restrictions by allowing a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to accumulate eligible SR&ED expenditures in an undeducted pool and deduct any portion—from 0% to 100%—against business income in the current taxation year, carrying any remaining positive balance forward indefinitely to future taxation years9.
Mechanics of Subsection 37(1): Additions and Reductions

The CRA administers the Subsection 37(1) pool as a continuous running total without tracking the vintage of individual expenditure years9. The pool balance available for deduction at the end of a taxation year (reported on Line 455 of Form T661) is computed by adding specified positive components and subtracting mandatory reductions9.

The statutory additions to the Subsection 37(1) pool comprise five primary categories. First, Paragraph 37(1)(a) adds expenditures of a current nature incurred in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada, whether directly undertaken by the taxpayer (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), paid to a contractor performing SR&ED on the taxpayer’s behalf (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), paid as a third-party payment to a Canadian-resident corporation (Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.1)), or paid as a third-party payment to an approved university, college, research institute, or non-profit SR&ED corporation (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii))9. Under Bill C-15, current expenditures also include eligible equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 202421. Second, Paragraph 37(1)(b)—restored by Bill C-15 for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (following its repeal for property acquired from January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024)—adds capital expenditures for new or used depreciable property (excluding land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings) intended to be used all or substantially all (≥90%) in SR&ED in Canada8. Third, Paragraph 37(1)(c) adds amounts repaid in the taxation year in respect of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the Section 37 pool under Paragraph 37(1)(d)9. Fourth, Paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds back amounts included in the taxpayer’s income in a preceding taxation year by virtue of Paragraph 12(1)(v) (which forces a negative year-end Section 37 pool balance into taxable income), thereby resetting the opening pool balance to nil9. Fifth, Paragraph 37(1)(c.2) and Paragraph 37(1)(c.3) add the amount of any federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit recaptured and added to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable in the preceding taxation year under Subsections 127(27) to 127(30), including partnership ITC recapture excess amounts9.

The statutory reductions from the Subsection 37(1) pool likewise operate across five categories. First, Paragraph 37(1)(d) subtracts all government assistance (such as provincial R&D tax credits and federal or provincial grants like NRC IRAP) and non-government assistance that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date in respect of SR&ED expenditures included in the pool9. (Note: Contract payments received by an R&D performer reduce the Subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes under Subsection 127(18), but do not reduce the performer's Subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool because the contract revenue is included in the performer's business income under Section 9.)3. Second, Paragraph 37(1)(d.1) subtracts any provincial "super-allowance benefit amount" for the year or preceding taxation years9. Third, Paragraph 37(1)(e) subtracts the amount of federal SR&ED ITCs deducted from Part I tax payable and/or received as a cash refund in the preceding taxation year (reported on Line 435 of Form T661)9. Fourth, Paragraph 37(1)(f) and Paragraph 37(1)(f.1) subtract amounts deducted from the pool in computing income in preceding taxation years under Subsection 37(1) or deducted with respect to insolvency under Section 61.39. Fifth, Paragraph 37(1)(h) applies reductions mandated under Subsection 37(6.1) upon an acquisition of control (a loss restriction event)9.
Taxability of the SR&ED ITC: Interaction of Paragraph 37(1)(e), Paragraph 12(1)(t), and Paragraph 12(1)(v)

A critical audit verification rule is that federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits are themselves effectively taxable, but on a one-year deferred basis3. When a claimant earns and claims an SR&ED ITC (either as a cash refund under Section 127.1 or as an offset against Part I tax under Subsection 127(5)) in Year 1, that credit reduces the claimant’s Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in Year 2 under Paragraph 37(1)(e)3. If the claimant deducted its entire Section 37 pool in Year 1 and incurs fewer new SR&ED expenditures in Year 2 than the Year 1 ITC reduction, the Year 2 Section 37 pool balance becomes negative at the end of Year 29. Under Paragraph 12(1)(v) (and Paragraph 12(1)(t) where an ITC is included in income in the following year), a negative Section 37 pool balance at year-end cannot be carried forward as a negative number; the full negative balance must be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income for Year 2, and Paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds an equal amount back in Year 3 to restore the pool to zero3. Furthermore, where a claimant elects the Proxy Method and earns a federal ITC on the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), that ITC still reduces the Section 37 pool in the following year under Paragraph 37(1)(e) even though the PPA itself was never added to the Section 37 pool3.
Related Businesses, Exclusive Economic Zone, Foreign SR&ED, and Loss Restriction Events

Where a corporate claimant performs SR&ED in Canada that relates not to its own active business, but to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (for example, a dedicated R&D subsidiary performing research for an operating parent or sister corporation at the time the expenditure is incurred), Subsection 37(1.1) deems the SR&ED to relate to a business of the claimant (determined without reference to control by right)9. Under Subsection 37(1.3), SR&ED carried out in the Exclusive Economic Zone of Canada is eligible on the same basis as domestic SR&ED9. Conversely, under Subsection 37(2), expenditures for research carried on outside Canada are deductible as current business expenses in the year incurred, but they cannot be added to the Subsection 37(1) pool and do not earn any federal ITC—with the sole exception of "permissible salary or wages" paid to Canadian-resident employees performing support SR&ED outside Canada up to the limit determined under Subsection 37(1.5)4.

When control of a corporation is acquired by a person or group of persons (or a trust experiences a change in majority-interest beneficiary), Subsection 37(6.1) and Paragraph 37(1)(h) trigger a loss restriction event: a deemed taxation year-end occurs immediately before the acquisition of control, and the undeducted Subsection 37(1) pool is reduced to nil unless the "streaming" conditions of Subsection 37(6.1) are satisfied9. Specifically, the pre-acquisition SR&ED pool can be reinstated and carried forward for deduction in post-acquisition years only if: (1) the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit throughout the subsequent year, and (2) the deduction is limited to the corporation's income for that year (before deducting the SR&ED pool) derived from that same business or a similar business9. Additionally, under Subsection 37(4) and Regulation 2902(c), no Section 37 deduction or Section 127 ITC is permitted for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (preventing double-claiming between the R&D performer and an IP buyer)9. Under Subsection 37(5), any payment that qualifies as both an SR&ED expenditure and a charitable gift under Section 110.1 or Section 118.1 must be deducted exclusively under Section 37 and cannot be claimed as a charitable donation9.

body.text: Section 2: Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Outs, Refundability, and Carryforwards
2.1 Basic (15%) vs. Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates

Under Subsection 127(9) and Subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act, the federal SR&ED program operates a two-tier Investment Tax Credit rate structure applied to a claimant’s net SR&ED qualified expenditure pool (Line 570 of Form T661)6. The Basic ITC Rate (15%) applies to: (a) all corporations that are neither Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) nor Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—including Canadian subsidiaries controlled by foreign parent corporations and large public companies exceeding the phase-out thresholds; (b) qualified expenditures of a CCPC or ECPC that exceed its annual expenditure limit; (c) individuals (sole proprietorships) and trusts; and (d) all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a partnership (calculated at the partnership level and allocated to eligible partners under Subsection 127(8))10.

By contrast, the Enhanced ITC Rate (35%) applies to qualifying CCPCs and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), which earn an additional 20% enhancement under Subsection 127(10.1) on top of the 15% basic rate, yielding a combined 35% enhanced ITC rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit6.
2.2 The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Dual Phase-Out Formulas under Bill C-15

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit was $3,000,000 (generating a maximum enhanced ITC of $1,050,000) and was restricted exclusively to CCPCs, phasing out linearly when the associated group’s prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lay between $10,000,000 and $50,000,0004. Under Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026), for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000, allowing an eligible CCPC or ECPC to earn up to $2,100,000 per year at the 35% enhanced rate4. (Note: While the December 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the expenditure limit to $4.5 million, Federal Budget 2025 raised the limit to $6.0 million effective retroactively for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, which was enacted into law by Bill C-15.)8. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is subject to reduction under one of two statutory phase-out methods detailed in the CRA’s SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026)4.
Method A: Prior-Year Taxable Capital Phase-Out (Default for CCPCs — Subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21) ITA)

Unless a CCPC elects to use the revenue method, its $6,000,000 expenditure limit (shared across all associated corporations) begins to decrease once its taxable capital employed in Canada for the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated (reduced to nil) when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,0004. Across this $60,000,000 phase-out range ($75,000,000 minus $15,000,000), the expenditure limit is reduced proportionally as prior-year taxable capital rises above $15,000,0006:

For example, if an associated CCPC group had $30,000,000 of taxable capital employed in Canada in the preceding taxation year ($15,000,000 above the $15,000,000 floor, or one-quarter of the $60,000,000 phase-out range), its expenditure limit for the current year is reduced by $1,500,000, leaving an enhanced expenditure limit of $4,500,000 (generating up to $1,575,000 of ITCs at 35%, with any qualified expenditures above $4,500,000 earning the 15% basic rate)6.
Method B: Three-Year Average Annual Gross Revenue Phase-Out (Mandatory for ECPCs under Subsection 127(10.6); Elective for CCPCs under Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) ITA)

Because public corporations and capital-intensive technology or manufacturing companies often carry substantial balance-sheet capital while still being pre-revenue or mid-sized in commercial scale, Bill C-15 introduced an alternative Average Annual Revenue phase-out test4. An Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—defined in Subsection 127(9) as a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange that is resident in Canada and is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (even if all shares owned by non-residents were instead owned by a single person)—must calculate its $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the revenue method under Subsection 127(10.6)6. Under Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a standalone CCPC or an associated group of CCPCs, respectively, may also elect on a prescribed form to compute its expenditure limit using the 3-year average gross revenue method instead of the taxable capital method4.

Under the revenue method, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to phase out when the corporation’s (or consolidated/associated group’s) average annual revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil at $75,000,000 or greater4. Average annual revenue is determined from the financial statements (or consolidated financial statements as defined in Subsection 233.8(1) for an ECPC group) of every member of the group for the 3 preceding fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire 3-year window, including each corporation's reasonable share of partnership or trust revenues and permitting reasonable adjustments (such as eliminating intra-group sales of goods or services) so that the annual revenue reflects that of a single economic entity6.
Proration for Short Tax Years and Allocation Among Associated / Consolidated Groups

If a corporation’s taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks, its calculated expenditure limit must be prorated by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365: Prorated Limit = Expenditure Limit × (Number of days in the tax year ÷ 365)6. Special rules under Subsections 127(10.5) and 127(10.64) also apply where a corporation has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year or is associated in two or more tax years ending in the same calendar year6. Associated CCPCs must file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under Subsection 127(10.3) to apportion their shared expenditure limit4. Members of a consolidated ECPC group (and CCPCs electing the revenue method) must similarly file a joint allocation agreement (maintaining working papers until the CRA's dedicated Fall 2026 revenue-allocation schedule is filed)6. If an associated or consolidated group fails to file an allocation agreement within 30 days of a written request by the CRA, the CRA may assign an expenditure limit of nil or allocate it among the group6.
2.3 Refundability Rules Across Claimant Categories (Section 127.1 ITA)

Under Section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, a claimant that has no Part I federal income tax payable (or whose earned SR&ED ITC exceeds its Part I tax payable) may receive all or a portion of its unused current-year SR&ED ITC as a direct cash refund6. However, refundability depends strictly on: (1) the legal status of the claimant (Qualifying Corporation, Excluded Corporation, other CCPC, ECPC, other corporation, individual/trust, or partnership member); (2) whether the expenditure is within or above the annual expenditure limit; and (3) whether the expenditure is of a current nature or a capital nature (including Shared-Use Equipment)6.

A critical distinction in the Income Tax Act is the difference between a "Qualifying Corporation", an "Excluded Corporation", and a "CCPC other than a Qualifying or Excluded Corporation" for purposes of the 40% refundability of the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit6. Under Subsection 127.1(2) and the CRA’s SR&ED Glossary and SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, a Qualifying Corporation is a CCPC (stand-alone or associated) whose prior-year taxable income (combined with all associated corporations) did not exceed its qualifying income limit, determined by the statutory formula $500,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (including that of associated corporations) is ≤ $15,000,000, or otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of that taxable capital over $15,000,000, so that the qualifying income limit is reduced to nil once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 (before the Bill C-15 amendments, the formula used $40,000,000 in place of $60,000,000 and a $10,000,000 threshold)10. While prior-year taxable income does not restrict a CCPC from earning the 35% enhanced rate up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, "Qualifying Corporation" status still governs whether a CCPC can obtain a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit (or when allocated a 15% ITC from a partnership)10. For an Excluded Corporation, the refund rate on the 35% enhanced ITC on current expenditures is 40% rather than 100%10. Furthermore, because a partnership is not a taxpayer, SR&ED ITCs on partnership expenditures are always calculated at the 15% basic rate at the partnership level and allocated to partners who are not "specified members" (i.e., general partners actively engaged in the partnership business)10. A partner that is a CCPC cannot claim the 35% enhanced rate on partnership expenditures, and its allocated 15% partnership ITC is 40% refundable only if the CCPC is a Qualifying Corporation (otherwise it is non-refundable)10.

body.text: 2.4 Carryback, Carryforward, Deemed Deductions, and Loss of CCPC Status

Under Subsection 127(5) of the Income Tax Act, any portion of an SR&ED ITC that is not used to offset Part I tax payable in the current taxation year and is not refunded in cash under Section 127.1 may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable4. If an unused ITC is not applied within the 20-year carryforward window, it expires permanently27. Furthermore, any SR&ED ITC that is refunded to the taxpayer in the taxation year is deemed under Subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted from Part I tax otherwise payable under Subsection 127(5), thereby reducing the balance of the ITC pool available for carryback or carryforward and triggering the subsequent-year Section 37 pool reduction under Paragraph 37(1)(e)6.

Because CCPC status turns on control rather than mere share ownership, executing a financing agreement, option, or shareholders' agreement that gives non-residents or public corporations a right to acquire control can cause the corporation to lose CCPC status for the taxation year, reducing its federal SR&ED rate from 35% refundable to 15% non-refundable10.

3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method: Election Mechanics and Strategic Trade-Offs

Under the CRA’s Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy (updated March 30, 2022), the election is made for each taxation year and applies across all SR&ED projects claimed in that year26.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages: Eligibility, Specified Employee Caps, Foreign Work, and the 180-Day Rule

Governed by the CRA’s SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), labour expenditures typically represent the largest component of Canadian SR&ED claims33. Under Subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA (which could relate to gross wages reported on a T4 slip)39.

For non-specified employees, SR&ED salary or wages generally include regular salary and wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, tips/gratuities, honoraria, directors’ fees, management fees, commissions, inducements/non-competition payments, and taxable benefits under Section 6 (such as automobile benefits, group term life insurance, housing/board/meals, gifts/awards, low-interest loans, or tuition fees, provided there is a cash outlay or a reasonable estimate of actual costs excluding GST/HST/PST unless no input tax credit can be claimed, and the actual costs are not also claimed as a regular business expense)39. Conversely, five categories of employee-related payments are strictly excluded from SR&ED salary or wages: (1) the employer's share of related benefits (CPP, QPP, EI, provincial workers' compensation [WSIB/CNESST], approved pension plans, and non-taxable medical/dental/optical plans), which can only be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method31; (2) amounts for extended vacation or extended sick leave (considered not directly engaged in or undertaking/supervising/supporting SR&ED)39; (3) stock option benefits (considered not to be an expenditure for SR&ED)39; (4) retiring allowances / severance payments (excluded from salary/wages under Subsection 248(1), though potentially claimable as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method)31; and (5) payments to partners of a partnership, because a member cannot be an employee of a partnership for income tax purposes and any payment to a partner is treated as a distribution of partnership income37.

Whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is a question of fact based on the tasks performed rather than the employee's job title27. Eligible directly engaged tasks include hands-on experimentation, prototype fabrication, testing, mathematical or engineering analysis, direct technical supervision of SR&ED work (requiring a technological background based on academic or work experience, as opposed to general managerial administrative supervision), technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year (assigning technical personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, assessing material quality), and specific tasks performed by non-specialized employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine) when supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications3. Under the CRA's All or Substantially All (ASA) Rule, if all or substantially all (90% or more) of an employee's time is attributable to SR&ED in Canada, the entire eligible salary expenditure is included; otherwise, only the proportion of time spent on specific eligible SR&ED activities is claimable, supported by contemporaneous time records3.

A "specified employee"—broadly defined in Subsection 248(1) as an employee who owns 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation (or a related corporation) or does not deal at arm's length with the employer—is subject to two distinct statutory caps3:

items: Allowable SR&ED Salary Cap (Subsection 37(9.1) ITA): For a specified employee, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages, and the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages claimed cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days the individual was a specified employee in the taxation year3. If a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no SR&ED salary may be claimed unless the associated corporations file an allocation agreement on Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) accompanied by a certified copy of the directors' resolution delegating authority (or a signed confirmation if owned by a single sole shareholder)39.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap (Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9)): When calculating the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 to which the 55% PPA rate applies, the claimant must first exclude bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year for all employees (Lines 810–812)4. Then, for each specified employee (Lines 852–858), the amount included in the PPA salary base is restricted to the lesser of: (a) the actual directly engaged SR&ED salary (Line 852 total base salary × Line 854 SR&ED time % = Line 856); (b) 75% of the specified employee’s total salary or wages for the year (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages); or (c) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the corporation's taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the claimant employed the individual in the taxation year: 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in Year ÷ 365) (Line 858)4.

Under Subsection 37(1.5), a claimant may include "permissible salary or wages" for SR&ED work performed outside Canada only if all five statutory conditions are satisfied: (1) the work was performed directly by an employee of the claimant and not a contractor; (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work related to a business of the claimant; (4) the work outside Canada was an integral part and solely in support of an SR&ED project carried out in Canada; and (5) the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country9. Furthermore, under the Traditional Method, foreign travel, hotel, and meal overhead expenses relating to foreign SR&ED wages are disallowed31. Finally, under Subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary or wages not paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred are deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year for SR&ED purposes27.
3.3 Overhead and Other Expenditures: The 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount vs. Traditional Overhead

When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, it calculates a notional overhead substitute equal to 55% of its eligible Part 5 salary base under Regulation 2900(4) (reported on Line 820 of Part 5 and transferred to Line 502 of Part 4 of Form T661), subject to an overall PPA cap4. (Historical Note: The PPA rate was 65% for 2012 and earlier years, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% since 2014 ; claiming 65% overstates the proxy overhead by 10 percentage points.)4. Because the PPA is a notional amount, it is included only in Qualified Expenditures to earn the Section 127 ITC and is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool; instead, the claimant deducts its actual overhead outlays (utilities, office supplies, support salaries, employer payroll taxes) as regular business expenses4.

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, it claims actual overhead and other current expenditures on Line 360 of Form T6618. Under the CRA’s SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022) and Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3), every claimed overhead item (or allocated portion thereof) must be "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada), which requires passing two cumulative tests27. First, under the Directly Related Test, there must be a direct link—without any intervening step or intermediary—between the expenditure and either (a) the SR&ED work, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED31. Second, under the Incremental Test, the claimant bears the burden of proving that the expenditure (or claimed portion) would not have been incurred if the SR&ED work had not been carried out27. Fixed costs (such as a flat-rate annual equipment maintenance contract that does not change with usage) fail the incremental test and cannot be claimed by applying a flat percentage31. Variable costs (such as electricity, gas, or water that vary directly with equipment usage) or incremental clerical staffing (including where the aggregated SR&ED support time of multiple clerks equals a full position that would not otherwise have been needed, such as 5 clerks × 20% = 100% of one job) satisfy the incremental test31.

Three specialized Traditional Method overhead rules require careful verification during an audit. First, while the salaries of clerical and administrative staff (HR, accounting, purchasing) providing non-technological services to SR&ED employees can qualify on Line 360, the employer's share of related benefits (CPP, EI, WCB, medical insurance) for those clerical/administrative employees can never be claimed because the CRA considers them "overhead on overhead" (an indirect link), and training or travel costs for clerical/administrative staff are similarly disallowed31. Second, a retiring allowance (severance or retirement payment in recognition of long service or loss of office) qualifies on Line 360 only if it was part of the written employment contract of an employee who performed hands-on SR&ED and is allocated based on the ratio of allowable SR&ED wages to total career wages31. Third, under Subparagraph 2902(a)(i) of the Income Tax Regulations, current expenditures for the general administration or management of a business are "prescribed expenditures"31. Specifically, external professional fees paid to prepare an SR&ED claim (both the accounting and technical portions) are classified as prescribed expenditures: even if directly related and incremental (included in the Section 37 deductible pool), they must be deducted on Line 530/532 of Part 4 and cannot earn an SR&ED ITC (whereas in-house salary or wages paid to the claimant’s own employees for preparing the SR&ED claim are exempt from the prescribed expenditure exclusion under Clause 2902(a)(i)(A))8.
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed, Prototypes, Pilot Plants, and Production Runs

Governed by the CRA’s Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated December 18, 2014), SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (updated July 19, 2016), and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (updated July 19, 2016), materials are claimable under both the Proxy Method (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)) and Traditional Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(a))32.

The CRA defines "materials for SR&ED" strictly as physical, tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that, at a given moment in the SR&ED process, compose the body of a thing (a tangible object) on which SR&ED is being carried out or that results from the SR&ED being carried out27. Intangible items (such as data or software licences) and laboratory or shop supplies that do not compose the body of the object (such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes, cleaning supplies, used lubricants, CDs/DVDs, and general utilities like water, electricity, propane, or natural gas) are not materials for SR&ED (they may qualify only as overhead under the Traditional Method)41. Furthermore, the cost of materials (including service costs such as third-party galvanization required before testing a metal part) can only be claimed in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—never when merely purchased, received from a supplier, or removed from inventory—and must be paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year35.

The distinction between Materials Consumed and Materials Transformed controls whether subsequent disposition triggers ITC Recapture41. Materials Consumed are materials that were destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED (if experimental production is sold for more than 10% of the original cost, the materials are considered not to have been consumed)27. Consumed materials are 100% eligible and are not subject to ITC recapture41. Materials Transformed are materials that were not rendered virtually valueless after the SR&ED, but were physically transformed or incorporated into an experimental prototype, custom product, commercial asset, or experimental production output as a result of the SR&ED32. Transformed materials are 100% eligible in the year transformed, but if the resulting property is sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the cost of the purchased materials (excluding in-house labour and overhead) is subject to ITC recapture under Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)41. Under Subsection 127(11.6), if materials are purchased from a non-arm's length party, the qualified expenditure is restricted to the cost incurred by the non-arm's length party, excluding any intercompany profit element41.

When SR&ED involves physical assets or manufacturing facilities, the CRA classifies the context into Prototypes, Custom Products / Commercial Assets, Pilot Plants, or Production Runs (ED+EP vs. ED+CP)32. A prototype is an experimental trial model possessing the essential characteristics of an intended product, constructed to test a hypothesis and generally having no lasting commercial value; its design, construction, and testing labour and consumed materials are current SR&ED expenditures (duplicate prototype copies constructed for testing prior to commercial production are claimed as materials consumed or transformed when testing is completed, whereas duplicate copies built to establish commercial inventory are disallowed)32. A pilot plant is a non-commercial scale production facility isolated from normal business operations and used solely for SR&ED over its entire useful life (never converted to commercial production or sales demonstration); labour and materials consumed or transformed in resolving technological uncertainties and operating the pilot plant are allowable32.
When experimental development is conducted during a manufacturing production run, the CRA distinguishes between two contexts52:

items: Experimental Development Resulting in Experimental Production (ED+EP): Occurs when there is documented technical risk to the process or product (such as process instability, stoppages, equipment damage risk, or abnormal yield losses) and no simultaneous commercial production is taking place52. In an ED+EP run, salaries of directly engaged staff (including supervised non-specialized operators required to produce the experimental run) and materials consumed or transformed in the required experimental production are allowable, excluding any "excess production" beyond the quantity strictly required for the SR&ED27.

Experimental Development in Conjunction with Commercial Production (ED+CP): Occurs when SR&ED is conducted during regular commercial operations52. In an ED+CP run, all standard commercial production costs are excluded, and only incremental SR&ED salaries, incremental overhead, and incremental material loss/scrap (actual material loss minus standard commercial material loss) reasonably attributable to the experimental development are allowable52. Where it is impossible for both the claimant and the CRA to isolate SR&ED work from commercial work in a custom product/asset or an ED+CP run, the CRA permits an Administrative Alternative (Incremental Cost) Approach, provided the CRA agrees and the claimant signs a formal waiver of the right to object or appeal on that issue under Subsection 169(2.2) of the Income Tax Act32.

body.text: 3.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

One of the most significant reforms enacted by Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026) is the restoration of SR&ED tax incentives for capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, reversing the exclusion that applied from January 1, 2014 to December 15, 20248. These rules are governed by the CRA’s updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026)8.
A. SR&ED Capital Expenditures — The All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) Test

To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on Line 390 of Form T661, with the 10 most expensive properties per project listed on Lines 262–263 of Part 2 and the 20 most expensive listed in Part 6 Box 780), the expenditure must satisfy five requirements8:

items: Timing & Available-for-Use Rule (Subsection 37(1.2) and Subsection 13(27) ITA): The property must be acquired and become available for use after December 15, 2024 (property acquired or available for use before December 16, 2024, does not qualify)8.

Depreciable Property Ownership (Paragraph 20(1)(a) and Paragraph 37(1)(b) ITA): The expenditure must result in the claimant owning (or holding a leasehold interest in) depreciable property for which Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) could otherwise be claimed19. Land, inventory, goodwill, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded4. Additionally, under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF)—defined as desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, pagers, and calculators, but explicitly excluding computer hardware, software, and ancillary computer equipment—cannot be included8.

The ASA (≥90%) Intended Use Test (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) and (B)(III) ITA): At the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend either: (a) to use the property during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (b) to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada8.

New vs. Used Equipment Distinction (Paragraph 2902(b) ITR): Both new and used ASA depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, qualify for inclusion in the Subsection 37(1) Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures on Line 390 (providing up to 100% immediate deductibility in lieu of claiming regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8)8. However, used or refurbished property is a "prescribed expenditure" under Paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations and must be subtracted on Line 532 of Form T661—meaning only new ASA capital property qualifies to earn the Section 127 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit8.

40% Refundability on Capital ITCs: For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earning the 35% enhanced ITC up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the ITC earned on eligible new capital expenditures (and SUE) is 40% refundable in cash (14% effective cash refund, with the remaining 21% credit available to offset Part I tax or carry back 3 years / forward 20 years), compared to 100% refundability on current expenditures3.

body.text: (Complementary Accelerated CCA Measures): Where capital assets are not claimed in the Section 37 SR&ED pool, claimants may utilize: (a) the 100% first-year CCA deduction for Class 50 property (computers and systems software) acquired after April 15, 2024, and available for use before 20274; (b) temporary 100% immediate expensing for eligible Class 1 manufacturing and processing buildings (where ≥90% of floor space is used for manufacturing/processing) acquired on or after November 4, 2025, and first used before 2030 (phasing down to 75% in 2030–2031 and 55% in 2032–2033)14; and (c) the federal Productivity Mega Deduction announced in September–October 2026 expanding immediate expensing to over 65% of business assets54.
B. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — >50% to <90% Actual Operating Time)

When new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, is used for both SR&ED and commercial operations and therefore does not meet the ≥90% ASA test, it may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under Subsection 127(9) of the ITA (claimed on Line 504 of Form T661 under both the Proxy and Traditional Methods)8. To qualify, the property must be: (1) new depreciable property (never used, acquired to be used, or rented for any purpose before acquisition); (2) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024; (3) not ASA (≥90%) SR&ED capital property; (4) not General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF); and (5) not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Subsection 2900(11) of the Income Tax Regulations20. (Under Regulation 2900(11), property is disqualified as PDP if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended to use it for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a facility, plant, or line for commercial manufacturing/processing AND intended to use it during its operating time over its expected useful life primarily for non-SR&ED purposes.)20.

If the equipment is actually used primarily (more than 50% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period—which begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time—then it qualifies as First-Term SUE, and 25% (1/4) of the capital cost of the equipment (determined without borrowed money costs under Section 21 and adjusted for non-arm's length costs under Subsection 127(11.6)) is deemed to be a qualified SR&ED expenditure in that taxation year8. If the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and is actually used primarily (>50% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period—which begins when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time—then it qualifies as Second-Term SUE, and an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost is deemed to be a qualified expenditure in that second taxation year, for a maximum cumulative qualified expenditure inclusion of 50% of capital cost3. Unlike ≥90% ASA capital property, the capital cost of SUE is not part of the Section 37 SR&ED deductible pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the SUE asset on Schedule T2SCH8 under regular CCA rules, and any SUE ITC applied or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year8.
C. Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the CRA’s SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (where the underlying capital expenditure was made after December 15, 2024) are claimable according to the claimant's elected overhead method8:

items: Under the Traditional Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) ITA): If leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease expenditure can be claimed as a lease cost21. If leased equipment is used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED, the claimant can still include the proportional percentage of SR&ED usage on Line 360 as an overhead and other expenditure, provided the lease cost is directly related and incremental to SR&ED in Canada8. Under the Traditional Method, lease costs for GPOEF and the lease of land directly attributable to SR&ED are also allowable21.

Under the Proxy Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI) ITA): If leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost may be claimed21. If leased equipment (excluding GPOEF) is used more than 50% but less than 90% ("primarily") of its operating time in SR&ED in Canada, exactly 50% of the lease cost may be claimed21. If leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time in SR&ED, 0% is claimable under the Proxy Method (nor can lease of land or GPOEF be claimed)21.

Strict Exclusion of Building Leases (Paragraph 37(8)(d)/(e) ITA and Regulation 2903): Rent or lease outlays for the use of, or right to use, any building (defined as a structure with walls and a roof affixed to land affording protection and shelter) are excluded from SR&ED under both methods—with the sole exception of lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for a prescribed special-purpose building approved on a building-by-building basis by the Department of Finance Canada under Section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations21.

body.text: 3.6 Subcontractors (SR&ED Contracts), Non-Arm's Length Transfers, Third-Party Payments, and Recapture

When a claimant contracts an arm's-length party to perform SR&ED in Canada on the claimant's behalf (where the payer controls the work, owns the exclusive rights, and bears the risk), 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (Line 340 of Form T661), but only 80% is included in Qualified Expenditures to earn the Section 127 ITC (with 20% subtracted on Line 529 of Part 4)3. To qualify for the 80% ITC inclusion, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" (payments to non-taxable suppliers are deducted in full on Line 528)26. Furthermore, under the Look-Through Rule in Subsections 37(14) and 37(15), the payer's contract expenditure must be reduced by any non-current expenditure incurred by the performer, and the performer is required to notify the payer in writing without delay if requested, or no later than 90 days after the end of the calendar year8.

When a claimant (payer) enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer under Section 251, the payer's expenditures are allowable in its Section 37 deductible pool, but Paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in Subsection 127(9) excludes the entire NAL contract payment from the payer's ITC calculation (0% ITC)30. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures, and the payment received from the NAL payer is not treated as a "contract payment" that reduces the performer's qualified expenditures30. Alternatively, under Subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer all or part of the performer's qualified expenditures (reported on Line 540/546 of the performer's T661 and Line 510 of the payer's T661), capped at the lesser of the contract amount or what the performer's qualified expenditure pool would have been at year-end8. (Under Subsection 127(15), if the performer attempts to transfer more than its qualified expenditure pool, no amount can be transferred; under Subsection 127(13), partnerships cannot transfer or receive expenditures via Form T1146; under Subsection 127(16), transfers are reduced to nil if the parties became NAL primarily to use Form T1146; and under Subsection 127(24), interposing an arm's-length party between a payer and a NAL performer is ineffective.)30.

Governed by the CRA’s Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a third-party payment (Subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii) ITA) differs from an SR&ED contract: in a third-party payment, the payer makes a payment (in cash, funding for students/employees, or payments in kind at fair market value) to an Approved Entity (approved university, college, research institute, association, or granting council) or to a non-profit SR&ED corporation or other corporation resident in Canada (Entities A to E) for SR&ED carried on in Canada where the performer controls the research and rights are non-exclusive (generally published), provided the research relates to a business of the claimant and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results33. Third-party payments are recognized on a cash basis, require filing a separate Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment, are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (Line 370), and are 80% eligible for the Section 127 ITC (20% subtracted on Line 529)26.

Under Subsection 127(26), if any SR&ED expenditure other than salary or wages (such as a contract expenditure, material purchase, or overhead bill) is not paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year, 100% of that unpaid expenditure is deemed not to have been incurred in that year for ITC purposes (subtracted on Line 520 of Part 4 of Form T661)26. When the expenditure is paid in a subsequent taxation year, the eligible portion (100% for materials/overhead; 80% for arm's-length contracts) is added back on the "payment of prior years' unpaid amounts (other than salary or wages)" line of Form T661 in the year of payment—provided the unpaid expenditure was identified on Form T661 by the SR&ED reporting deadline for the year it was originally incurred40.

Finally, under Subsections 127(27) to 127(36) and the CRA’s Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 14, 2022), if a claimant acquired property in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years by Subsection 127(36)), claimed the cost as a qualified SR&ED expenditure that generated an ITC (including materials transformed, post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital property, post-December 15, 2024 SUE, pre-2014 capital/SUE, or tangible property acquired through an SR&ED contract), and subsequently disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the ITC is recaptured8. The recaptured amount (the lesser of the ITC earned on the property or the ITC rate multiplied by the proceeds of disposition [arm's-length sale] or fair market value [commercial conversion or NAL disposition]) is added directly to Part I tax payable for the year of disposition/conversion (via Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)), and an equal amount increases the claimant's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the following taxation year under Paragraph 37(1)(c.2)8. (Audit Planning Rule: If a company manufactures an experimental part in-house and later sells it, there is no recapture on the in-house salaries or overhead —only the cost of purchased materials transformed is recaptured; conversely, if the company orders the part from an arm's-length supplier for $12,000, the full $12,000 cost is subject to recapture!)42.
Section 4: Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Federal Innovation Grant Stacking
4.1 Statutory Grinding Mechanics under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(18)

Canadian tax law permits businesses to stack non-repayable government grants, wage subsidies, and provincial R&D tax credits alongside federal SR&ED claims, while preventing double recovery on the same dollar of outlay through the statutory reduction rules in Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, audited under the CRA’s Assistance and Contract Payments Policy36.

Under Subsection 127(9), "government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (an entity that has a duty to the public, is subject to a significant degree of government control, and uses its profits for the benefit of the public)—including assistance from a Crown corporation, a foreign government, or indirect assistance routed through a government-funded non-profit entity—whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including provincial/territorial R&D tax credits), investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, other than the federal SR&ED ITC36. If loan repayments are non-firm, conditional upon future project revenue, or feature repayment ceilings and fixed end-dates regardless of full repayment, the CRA treats the contributions as government assistance (forgivable loans) rather than business debt36. "Non-government assistance" is any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance that would be included in income under Paragraph 12(1)(x)36. "Contract payments" are amounts paid or payable by an arm's-length taxable supplier (for SR&ED performed for or on its behalf) or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or Part I tax-exempt entity for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf27.

Under Subsection 127(18), qualified SR&ED expenditures for a taxation year are reduced on an accrual basis by all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year36. This reduction is applied strictly on a project-by-project basis: assistance or contract payments for one project cannot reduce the expenditures of another project (though excess assistance on a single project carries forward to reduce future years' expenditures on that same project, or reduces a non-arm's length affiliate's qualified expenditures on that same project under Subsection 127(19), which may be allocated using Form T1145 under Subsection 127(20))8. When government or non-government assistance is subsequently repaid, the repayment increases the Section 37 deductible pool under Paragraph 37(1)(c) and earns an ITC (at the original year's ITC rate) on Line 560 of Form T661, though the ITC earned on a repayment is non-refundable6.

Crucially, under the Proxy Method, because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 is calculated on the gross eligible SR&ED salary base before subtracting government grants, and the grant is subtracted only in Part 4 from the combined total of salaries plus PPA, the claimant retains the full 55% notional overhead credit on the grant-funded salaries26. Furthermore, under the CRA’s Assistance and Contract Payments Policy (Section 4.5), while a provincial R&D tax credit earned on the PPA reduces federal qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under Subsection 127(18), the portion of the provincial credit that relates to the notional PPA does not reduce the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool under Paragraph 37(1)(d) (because the PPA is not in the Section 37 pool); instead, that portion of the provincial credit is included directly in taxable income in the year received under Paragraph 12(1)(x)36.
