body.text: 4.3 Step-by-Step Mathematical Demonstration of Grant + SR&ED Stacking (CCPC under Proxy Method)

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of stacking NRC IRAP with the federal 35% SR&ED ITC (and a 10% British Columbia refundable SR&ED credit), consider a qualifying CCPC in British Columbia (tax year beginning January 1, 2025) that incurs $100,000 in direct, hands-on SR&ED salaries for non-specified employees on a single eligible project and receives an 80% NRC IRAP contribution ($80,000) toward those salaries26:

items: Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Form T661, Part 3, Line 380 / Line 400): Direct SR&ED Salaries and Wages = $100,00026.

Prescribed Proxy Amount Calculation (Form T661, Part 5, Line 820 → Part 4, Line 502): Eligible Salary Base (unreduced by government assistance) = $100,00026. Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) at 55% (Regulation 2900(4)) = $100,000 × 55% = $55,0004.
Gross Qualified Expenditures Before Assistance: $100,000 (Salaries) + $55,000 (PPA) = $155,00026.
Reduction for NRC IRAP Grant (Form T661, Part 4, Line 515): Gross Qualified Expenditures ($155,000) minus NRC IRAP Contribution ($80,000) = $75,00026.
British Columbia SR&ED Refundable Tax Credit (Form T666 — 10%): B.C. Qualifying Expenditure Base = $75,000; B.C. Refundable SR&ED Credit at 10% = $75,000 × 10% = $7,50017.

Federal Qualified SR&ED Expenditures After Provincial Credit Grind (Form T661, Part 4, Line 513 & Line 570): Under Subsection 127(18), the $7,500 B.C. credit is government assistance that reduces federal qualified expenditures: $75,000 − $7,500 = $67,50036.
Federal Enhanced SR&ED Refundable ITC (Schedule T2SCH31 — 35%): $67,500 × 35% = $23,62510.

Total Combined Non-Dilutive Cash Recovery: $80,000 (NRC IRAP) + $7,500 (B.C. SR&ED) + $23,625 (Federal SR&ED) = $111,125 (111.125% of the $100,000 direct salary outlay, covering 100% of the direct salary cost plus $11,125 toward actual un-tracked overhead)26.

body.text: Section 5: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes (2025–2026 Comparative Analysis)

Nine Canadian provinces and Yukon provide provincial or territorial R&D tax credits (or grants calculated through the corporate tax system) that stack on top of the federal SR&ED program, while three jurisdictions (Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut) offer no separate territorial or provincial R&D tax credit11. Because every provincial or territorial R&D tax credit constitutes government assistance under Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, claiming a provincial credit reduces the federal qualified SR&ED expenditure base dollar-for-dollar in the year earned (unless formally renounced or waived by the filing-due date)36.

Following the enactment of the federal Bill C-15 reforms ($6 million expenditure limit, $15M–$75M phase-out range, ECPC eligibility, and restored capital expenditures after December 15, 2024), Canadian provinces split into three distinct groups: express followers (British Columbia), targeted or independent restructurers (Québec with its new CRIC regime and Saskatchewan with its doubled $2 million cap), and structural holdouts (such as Ontario, Alberta, and Manitoba, which retained their existing expenditure limits and phase-out formulas)17.
5.1 Québec: The 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul (Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization)

In its March 25, 2025 Budget Speech, the Gouvernement du Québec enacted a comprehensive overhaul of provincial innovation tax assistance, introducing the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC) for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 202515. Administered by Revenu Québec (while maintaining harmonization with the federal definition of R&D and relying on the CRA for the scientific review of core R&D activities), the CRIC abolished and replaced seven legacy Québec R&D tax measures (for which transitional claims remain available only for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning before March 26, 2025)15:

items: The Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages of Researchers (R&D) (which previously provided 14% basic and up to 30% for CCPCs on the first $3,000,000 of R&D wages, subject to an asset-based excluded expenditures threshold of $50,000 to $225,000)16;
The Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium (which previously included 80% of contract amounts)16;
The Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium16;
The Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research16;
The Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services16;
The Industrial Design Component of the Design Tax Credits (note that the fashion design component continues to be eligible)16; and
The Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts16.

body.text: Core Architecture and Rules of the Québec CRIC (Taxation Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

The CRIC is 100% refundable for all eligible corporations operating a business in Québec with an establishment there15. Under official Gouvernement du Québec and Revenu Québec publications, the CRIC provides a two-tier rate structure without an asset test: a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of qualified R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures that exceed the applicable exclusion threshold (for eligible / Canadian-controlled corporations), and a 20% refundable rate on all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 maximum (and as the basic rate for other claimants, up from the legacy 14% rate)15.

Unlike the federal SR&ED program—which restricts eligibility to basic research, applied research, and experimental development and excludes style changes, routine testing, and commercial design under Paragraphs 248(1)(f), (i), and (j)—the Québec CRIC covers both eligible R&D activities and eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec, provided the pre-commercialization activities are undertaken in conjunction with (as a continuation of) R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation15. Eligible pre-commercialization activities encompass three areas: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation; (2) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials; and (3) quality control activities strictly to the extent they relate to the implementation of a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification15.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC comprise four cost categories incurred for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec: (1) 100% of salaries and wages paid to the corporation's employees; (2) 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec; (3) 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, an eligible research consortium, or an eligible university entity (reduced from the legacy 80% university rate to align with the 50% subcontracting rate); and (4) capital property acquisition costs for depreciable property acquired for eligible activities in Québec, excluding acquisition costs for a building, land, or a right to use a building or land15. Under Québec's anti-cumulation rules, a corporation cannot claim both the CRIC and another Québec tax credit (such as the Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation [C3i]) on the same expenditure, nor can a corporation holding an initial qualification certificate for a Large Investment Project tax holiday claim the CRIC for property used or acquired to be used in that project15.

To claim the CRIC, a corporation’s qualified expenditures in the taxation year must exceed an applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of: (1) $50,000; or (2) the sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable personal income tax system (reported in industry guides as $18,571 / $18,751 per FTE) for each employee, adjusted (prorated) to reflect the actual percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities15. Eligible corporations claim the CRIC by filing prescribed Form RD-1029.8.CR-T attached to their Québec corporate income tax return15.
5.2 Ontario: The Three-Pillar Regime (Taxation Act, 2007, S.O. 2007, c. 11)

Ontario operates three distinct corporate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the Canada Revenue Agency and claimed on provincial schedules attached to the T2 return59. All three require the corporation to maintain a permanent establishment in Ontario, perform eligible SR&ED in Ontario, and file a timely federal Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 within the 18-month reporting deadline59. Notably, Ontario retained its separate $3,000,000 expenditure limit and legacy phase-out thresholds rather than adopting the federal $6,000,000 cap17:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Taxation Act, 2007; Schedule 566; Schedule 5 Line 468): The OITC provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years), yielding a maximum annual cash refund of $240,00059. The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit is progressively reduced by two phase-out grinds across the associated group: (a) it begins to phase out when prior-year federal taxable income exceeds $500,000 and reaches nil at $800,000; and (b) it begins to phase out when prior-year specified capital employed in Canada reaches $25,000,000 and reaches nil at $50,000,00017. Under Subsection 96(14) of the Taxation Act, 2007, a corporation may waive/renounce the OITC in whole or in part36.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Section 45 and related provisions, Taxation Act, 2007; Schedule 508; Schedule 5 Line 416): The ORDTC provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced by any OITC or OBRITC claimed), with no expenditure limit and open to all corporations59. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 years and forward 20 years to offset Ontario corporate income tax otherwise payable, and converting R&D property to commercial use triggers ORDTC recapture under Section 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (calculated on Schedule 508 and reported on Line 277 of Schedule 5)17. Because an un-renounced ORDTC reduces the federal 35% refundable SR&ED base as government assistance under Subsection 127(18), corporations in a tax loss position may elect to renounce the ORDTC on or before the T2 filing-due date36. (Note on Ontario Capital Expenditures: While one October 2026 CPA commentary notes that Ontario restored capital expenditures acquired on or after December 16, 2024 for the OITC and ORDTC in line with the federal base59, other October 2026 advisory analyses note that published CRA OITC summaries still describe the OITC base as covering current expenditures without yet confirming the addition of restored capital expenditures17; claimants should verify Schedule 566/508 line instructions when filing.)

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Taxation Act, 2007; Schedule 568 + Schedule 569; Schedule 5 Line 470): The OBRITC provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under an eligible R&D contract with an eligible Ontario research institute (Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence and Networks of Centres of Excellence), up to an annual qualified expenditure cap of $20,000,000 (shared among associated corporations), for a maximum refundable credit of $4,000,000 per year59. Claimants file Schedule 568 plus a separate Schedule 569 for each eligible contract59.

body.text: 5.3 British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Atlantic Canada, and Yukon

British Columbia (Form T666) expressly aligned its provincial SR&ED tax credit with the principal federal Bill C-15 changes for taxation years beginning after December 15, 202417. Qualifying CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) can claim a 10% refundable credit on up to $6,000,000 of qualifying B.C. SR&ED expenditures (doubled from the prior $3,000,000 limit, raising the maximum refundable B.C. credit from $300,000 to $600,000), subject to the newly aligned $15,000,000 to $75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital phase-out and including restored post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures17. Expenditures above $6,000,000 and expenditures of non-CCPCs/non-ECPCs qualify for B.C.'s 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years)17. Furthermore, B.C. Budget 2026 removed the credit's sunset date, making the B.C. SR&ED tax credit permanent17. It is claimed on Form T666 within 18 months of tax year-end64.

Alberta (Innovation Employment Grant [IEG] — Sections 26.95 to 26.99, Alberta Corporate Tax Act) operates independently of the federal $6,000,000 changes, as confirmed by updated Alberta IEG guidance published on June 30, 2026 (Information Circular IEG-1)17. Administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance on the Alberta AT1 return, the IEG provides an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation’s base level of spending (calculated as the average of the corporation's qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the 2 preceding taxation years), plus an additional 12% incremental benefit—producing a combined 20% refundable rate—on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds the 2-year historical base17. The IEG is capped at $4,000,000 of annual eligible Alberta R&D spending, phases out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital, reduces the federal SR&ED pool and qualified expenditures as government assistance, and has a statutory filing deadline of 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date (with no carryback or carryforward)17.

Saskatchewan (Schedule 403) enacted a targeted province-specific expansion: for qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024, Saskatchewan doubled its refundable expenditure threshold for Saskatchewan CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000, providing a 10% refundable credit on the first $2,000,000 of annual qualifying expenditures (up to $200,000 refundable, without extending refundability to ECPCs)17. Qualifying expenditures above $2,000,000 for CCPCs, as well as qualifying expenditures of non-CCPCs, earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carrying back 3 years and forward 10 years), subject to an overall combined cap of $1,000,000 in total Saskatchewan R&D credits per year17.

Manitoba (Schedule 380) provides a 15% R&D tax credit with no expenditure limit, administered by the CRA and claimed on Schedule 380 within 1 year after the filing-due date17. Notably, Manitoba's eligible expenditure base never stopped including capital expenditures for depreciable property (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings)17. For in-house SR&ED in Manitoba, 50% of the credit (7.5% effective rate) is refundable and 50% (7.5% rate) is non-refundable (carrying back 3 years and forward 20 years), whereas for eligible R&D conducted under an eligible contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute, 100% of the 15% credit is refundable17.

Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301), and Yukon (Schedule 442) each provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no expenditure cap, available to all corporations (both CCPCs and foreign-controlled or public corporations)5. Yukon provides an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on eligible R&D expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University17. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick include property recapture rules on Schedules 340 and 36017.

Section 6: Intellectual Property Commercialization and Patent Box Regimes in Canada
6.1 Federal Patent Box Consultations vs. the 2026 "Productivity Mega Deduction"

In April 2024, the Department of Finance Canada launched a formal public Consultation on Creating a Patent Box Regime alongside its two-phase consultation on modernizing the SR&ED program, and subsequently reiterated a commitment to introduce a federal patent box in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement54. However, when Federal Budget 2025 was tabled in November 2025, the federal government omitted both the proposed federal Patent Box regime and the proposed innovation flow-through share regime14. Instead, Budget 2025 channeled federal innovation support into doubling the SR&ED enhanced expenditure limit to $6 million (enacted via Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026) and allocating $22.5 million for the Patent Collective and $75 million for the NRC IP Assist Program8.

Throughout the July–September 2026 pre-budget consultations for Budget 2026 (tabled in November 2026), no federal income-based Patent Box legislation was introduced54. Instead, on September 15, 2026, and via formal draft legislative proposals announced on October 1, 2026, the Department of Finance introduced the Productivity Mega Deduction, a broad cost-based Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) measure expanding immediate expensing to over 65% of business assets—including patents and software alongside pipelines, vehicles, and roads54. Consequently, as of November 2026, Canada does not operate a federal income-based Patent Box regime; preferential corporate income tax rates on commercialized IP income exist strictly at the provincial level in Québec and Saskatchewan16.
6.2 Provincial Patent Box Regimes: Québec (DCI) and Saskatchewan (SCII)

Québec’s Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (DCI) allows an eligible corporation to benefit from an effective Québec provincial corporate income tax rate of 2.0% (a 9.5 percentage point reduction compared to the general provincial corporate income tax rate of 11.5%) on the eligible portion of its taxable income derived from the commercialization of a qualifying intellectual property asset in Québec16. Following the introduction of the CRIC, Revenu Québec amended the Québec nexus ratio used to compute qualified profits under the DCI for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025: the Québec nexus ratio takes into account R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (unreduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold) rather than legacy R&D credits, while excluding expenditures for pre-commercialization activities from the nexus ratio calculation16.

Saskatchewan’s Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII / "Patent Box"), enacted under The Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (Patent Box) Act (S.S. c. S-10.2) and amended by The Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (Patent Box) Amendment Act, 2024 (Bill 158, published May 2024) and The Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (Patent Box) Amendment Act, 2025, lowers the Saskatchewan provincial Corporate Income Tax (CIT) rate from 12.0% down to 6.0% on income earned from the commercialization of qualifying intellectual property—including patents, trade secrets, and copyrights—that is new to the Canadian market45. Bill 158 amended Subsection 5(5) of the parent Act to extend the statutory benefit period from 7 years to 8 years (with program descriptions noting 10 to 15 years of eligibility where benchmark R&D was performed in Saskatchewan and a continuous application intake window open through June 30, 2027)84.
Section 7: Governing Bodies, Prescribed Forms, Statutory Deadlines, Review Procedures, and Penalties
7.1 Governing Authorities and Administrative Architecture

The Department of Finance Canada holds legislative policy responsibility for the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (including approving special-purpose SR&ED buildings under Regulation 2903)21. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers both the scientific/technical and financial compliance of the federal SR&ED program—as well as the provincial and territorial R&D tax credits of Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon12. Every CRA claim review is conducted by two specialist reviewers: a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates whether the claimed work meets the Subsection 248(1) eligibility criteria and reports to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who audits the claimed expenditures and reports to a Financial Review Manager [FRM])12. Revenu Québec independently administers the financial review and disbursement of the Québec CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T), while relying on the CRA for the scientific review of harmonized R&D15. Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration) independently administers the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) via the Alberta AT1 return47.
7.2 Prescribed Forms and the Updated May 2026 Form T661 (26) Architecture

Under the CRA’s SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and the updated forms released in May 2026 to implement Bill C-15, a claimant must file prescribed forms containing prescribed information to access SR&ED deductions and ITCs8.
Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), revised May 15, 2026 (T661 (26)), is structured into ten parts8:

items: Part 1 — General Information: Captures claimant identification and the election between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method on Lines 160 and 16222.

Part 2 — Project Information (Sections A to C): Requests the technical narrative for each project claimed (scientific or technological uncertainties, hypotheses formulated, chronological description of experiments/analyses conducted, and results/conclusions)22. Under the Top 20 Projects Rule, a claimant may choose to submit Part 2 with the claim for only the 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided that the claimant completes and maintains at its place of business a complete Part 2 for every project claimed (ready to submit upon CRA request; failure to provide it upon request results in disallowance of the project's expenditures) and includes the costs of every project in Part 622. Under the May 2026 update, Lines 262 and 263 require entering the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED depreciable capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024, used in each project8.

Part 3 — Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Sections A to C): Section B calculates allowable SR&ED expenditures, including directly engaged salaries/wages, materials consumed/transformed, SR&ED contracts (Line 340), Traditional Method overhead and proportional <90% equipment lease costs (Line 360), third-party payments (Line 370), total allowable current expenditures (Line 380), post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital expenditures including used equipment (Line 390), and total allowable SR&ED expenditures (Line 400)8. Section C calculates the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures, subtracting provincial government assistance (Line 429), other government assistance (Line 431), non-government assistance, and prior-year SR&ED ITCs applied and/or refunded (Line 435); adjusting for capital asset dispositions/recapture (Line 440), assistance repayments (Line 445), prior-year pool balance (Line 450), amalgamation/wind-up transfers (Line 452), and prior-year ITC recapture additions (Line 453) to determine the Amount Available for Deduction (Line 455), the Deduction Claimed in the Year (Line 460), and the Pool Balance Carried Forward (Line 470)8.

Part 4 — Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes: Starts with allowable current (Line 380) and capital (Line 390) expenditures; adds prior-year unpaid non-wage amounts paid in the year, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA — Line 502), First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Line 504), and NAL qualified expenditures transferred in via Form T1146 (Line 510); then subtracts provincial/territorial government assistance on current (Line 513) and post-Dec 15, 2024 capital/SUE (Line 514), other government assistance on current (Line 515) and capital (Line 516), non-government assistance and contract payments on current (Line 517) and capital (Line 518), current expenditures (other than wages) unpaid 180 days after year-end (Line 520), payments to non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), 20% of arm's-length contracts and third-party payments (Line 529), prescribed expenditures disallowed by regulation including claim preparation fees and used capital equipment (Lines 530 and 532), non-taxable income SR&ED costs (Lines 533 and 535), and NAL qualified expenditures transferred out via Form T1146 (Lines 540 and 546), yielding Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 559) plus assistance repayments (Line 560) = Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Line 570)8.

Part 5 — Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA): Computes the eligible salary base for non-specified employees (Lines 810–812, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits) and specified employees (Lines 852–858, applying the 75% and 2.5× YMPE caps), and multiplies the eligible salary base by 55% on Line 82022.

Part 6 — Project Costs: Mandatory project-by-project cost breakdown for all SR&ED projects claimed in the year (plus Box 780 naming the 20 most expensive post-Dec 15, 2024 capital and SUE properties)8.

Part 7 (Additional Information), Part 8 (Claim Checklist), Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information), and Part 10 (Certification): Part 9 requires prescribed information for every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the claim22. (Part 9 is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, and missing or inaccurate information in Part 9 does not disallow the SR&ED claim; however, a $1,000 penalty may be assessed for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable .)22.

body.text: 7.3 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline and Record Retention Rules

Under Subsection 37(11) (governing the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool) and Paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in Subsection 127(9) (governing the Section 127 ITC), a claimant must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) containing the prescribed information on or before the day that is 12 months after the claimant's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred4. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date under Paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after the end of its taxation year (whereas its balance of corporate tax is due 2 months—or 3 months for an eligible CCPC—after year-end under Paragraph 157(1)(b)), adding 12 months yields a corporate SR&ED reporting deadline of 18 months after the end of the taxation year (if a tax year ends on the last day of a month, the deadline is the last day of the 18th month; for example, for a December 31, 2024 corporate year-end, the absolute deadline is June 30, 2026)3. For individuals and trusts, the same statutory rule applies: the SR&ED reporting deadline (Form T661 plus Form T2038(IND)) is 12 months after the individual's or trust's income tax return filing-due date for the year22.

By explicit statutory exclusion in Subsection 220(2.2) of the Income Tax Act, there is no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion (including under the taxpayer relief provisions of Subsection 220(3.1)) to extend or waive the SR&ED reporting deadline3. If a claimant misses the reporting deadline for Form T661, the expenditures are permanently barred under Subsection 37(11.1) from being claimed as SR&ED expenditures or earning an ITC22. (Partial Filing Consequence: If a claimant files Form T661 on time by the reporting deadline, but files Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) after the reporting deadline, the claimant may still deduct the allowable SR&ED expenditures in its Section 37 pool, but is not entitled to earn any Section 127 Investment Tax Credit on those expenditures.)22. Under Section 230 and Paragraph 230(4)(b) of the Income Tax Act, claimants must retain all project and financial records for at least 6 years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate (and up to 20 years for property subject to ITC recapture under Subsection 127(27))4.
7.4 CRA Audit and Review Process, April 2026 Modernization, Objections, and Gross Negligence Penalties

Effective April 1, 2026, pursuant to Federal Budget 2025, the CRA implemented major administrative reforms to streamline SR&ED program operations8. First, the CRA launched an elective pre-claim approval process giving businesses upfront technical approval of their eligible SR&ED projects prior to filing (complementing the CRA's existing free Pre-Claim Consultation [PCC], Pre-Claim Review [PCR], permanent SR&ED Service Visit adopted June 20, 2023, and online Self-Assessment and Learning Tool [SALT])1. Second, for claims granted pre-claim approval that are selected for an expenditure-only review, the CRA's processing standard is reduced from 180 days down to 90 calendar days from the date the CRA receives a complete claim (standard refundable claims are targeted for processing within 60 to 120 days)12. Third, the CRA expanded its use of artificial intelligence in risk assessment to avoid subjecting low-risk claims to unnecessary audit interventions14.

When a filed SR&ED claim is selected for review, the audit follows three structured steps set out in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025 / April 20, 2026) and the CRA's Claim Review Manuals for RTAs and FRs12:

items: Step 1 — The Start of the Review: One of the assigned reviewers (RTA or FR) contacts the claimant by phone to provide reviewer contact details, confirm the official language of choice, outline the specific issues and projects selected for review, schedule a virtual (or exceptionally, on-site) review meeting, confirm secure digital communication channels (My Business Account, My Account, Represent a Client, or the CRA Secure Drop Zone launched January 15, 2024), and identify company participants12. This call is followed by an initial letter summarizing the discussion, providing a meeting agenda and manager contact information, and setting a deadline for any pre-meeting information requests following the Standard Timelines for Information Requests (generally 30 calendar days)12.

Step 2 — The Review Meeting and Requests for Additional Information: The RTA and FR conduct interviews with the technical and financial personnel who performed the work, tour the premises where applicable, review supporting contemporaneous documentation, share preliminary review findings at the conclusion of the meeting, and issue any additional information requests12.

Step 3 — The End of the Review, Administrative Second Review, and Formal Objection: The CRA issues its formal review findings on work eligibility and allowable expenditures12. If the claimant disagrees with the findings or has concerns with how the review was conducted, it may use the Dispute Resolution / Administrative Review Process (Form RC532, Request for Administrative Review, governed by the Guidelines for resolving claimants’ SR&ED concerns), under which the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and Financial Review Manager (FRM) review the file to ensure compliance with SR&ED legislation, policies, and due process1. If the claimant still disagrees with the final decision after the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has the statutory right to file a formal Notice of Objection within 90 days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada12.

body.text: Under Subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA’s Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), the CRA may assess a civil gross negligence penalty where a person knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes or participates in a false statement or omission in an initial or amended SR&ED claim33. The CRA carries the burden of proof under Subsection 163(3) on a balance of probabilities to show that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the Act (such as claiming normal business or personal expenses for SR&ED activities that did not take place, or continuing to claim non-qualifying projects, unsubstantiated amounts, or improper calculations after being advised in writing by the CRA that they do not qualify)38. When the gross negligence penalty applies, the penalty amount is the greater of $100 or 50% of the total of: (1) the understated Part I tax payable reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission under Paragraph 163(2)(a) (where overstated pool deductions and overstated ITCs are considered deducted first, and where taxable income is deemed not less than zero under Subsection 163(2.1) for understatements of income); plus (2) the refund of the overstated refundable ITC claimed by the claimant under Paragraph 163(2)(d) (calculated on the entire overstated refund regardless of what caused the overstatement once the gross negligence penalty applies)38.
Section 8: Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents on SR&ED

Canadian SR&ED tax administration is anchored in the binding jurisprudence of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). Canadian appellate courts have repeatedly held that while CRA administrative guidelines are non-binding, the five-part judicial test derived from Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is binding domestic law7.
8.1 Detailed Analysis of Controlling Canadian SR&ED Court Cases

items: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC): In the foundational judicial decision on SR&ED in Canada, Justice Bowman established the five core criteria (often summarized as the five-question approach) for determining whether a project constitutes eligible SR&ED under the Income Tax Act7: (1) Was there a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures (where "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field)? (2) Did the person claiming SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (3) Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? (4) Did the process result in a technological advancement (recognizing that the rejection of an unsuccessful hypothesis still constitutes a technological advancement if it advances general understanding recognizable to competent professionals)? (5) Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?7.

RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA): The Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed Justice Bowman’s Northwest Hydraulic approach while clarifying the evidentiary standard for Criterion 5 (Contemporaneous Documentation)7. The Court held that while documentary evidence recorded as the research progresses is highly advantageous and expected because scientific research requires repeatability, contemporaneous documentary evidence is not strictly mandatory as an absolute rule of law if the taxpayer adduces plausible, credible oral and other evidence that satisfies the court that eligible SR&ED was in fact conducted28.

C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393 (FCA): The Federal Court of Appeal (at paragraph 17) summarized the five criteria from Northwest Hydraulic (as approved in RIS-Christie) into the binding five-question framework used by the CRA and the courts to test SR&ED eligibility across all industries7.

Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC): Established the early Tax Court precedent distinguishing systematic investigation (trained observation, measurement, and methodical testing of hypotheses) from intuitive shop-floor trial and error29.

Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261, aff'd 2011 FCA 355 (FCA): A manufacturer of window coverings disputed the denial of SR&ED claims for developing new products and processes7. Justice D'Arcy of the Tax Court dismissed the appeal (affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal), ruling that although Jentel had provided sufficient documentation proving that it had undertaken a "systematic investigation", none of its activities qualified as SR&ED because the claim failed to prove technological risk/uncertainty or technological advancement24. Jentel confirms that thorough documentation of a systematic testing process cannot establish SR&ED eligibility if the underlying technical problem is solvable by standard practice24.

Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (TCC): The appellant contested the CRA's rejection of its SR&ED claim (for the 2008 and subsequent tax years) involving the development of a motor-activated hydraulic system to control the rate of descent of a theatre fire curtain in place of traditional counterweights29. The Tax Court agreed with the CRA that the problems could be solved through "routine engineering" and dismissed the appeal based on three key findings29: (1) Qualifications of Personnel: The research teams did not include any professional engineers or researchers holding a university degree or technical diploma in mechanical or hydraulic design, nor did they use specialized external resources or call trained researchers as witnesses24; (2) Formulation of Hypotheses: Defining a hypothesis as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial," the Court held that while hypotheses can be implicit across design iterations if reconstructible from the facts, they must be specific and innovative enough to distinguish a systematic investigation from simple trial and error28; and (3) Lack of Experimental Measurement: The Court emphasized that had the scientific method been used, the team would have determined the precise weight used in each experiment and precisely measured the duration of the curtain's descent across trials29. At the same time, the Court reaffirmed that contemporaneous detailed records, while beneficial, are not strictly mandatory29.

Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2019 TCC 246, aff'd 2021 FCA 88 (FCA): Appealing the denial of SR&ED claims for its 2009 and 2010 taxation years, the taxpayer argued before the Federal Court of Appeal that because the words "scientific method" do not appear in the statutory text of Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, the Tax Court Judge (Owen J.) erred in applying Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic7. Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Webb rejected this argument and dismissed the appeal, holding that Justice Bowman’s five criteria in Northwest Hydraulic (repeatedly endorsed by the FCA in RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel, and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc.) represent the binding judicial interpretation of the statutory definition of SR&ED in Subsection 248(1)7.

National R&D Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2020 TCC 47, aff'd 2022 FCA 72 (FCA): In this appeal by a consulting firm, the Tax Court found that the taxpayer satisfied only the first of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria (technological uncertainty) and failed the remaining four34. Writing for the Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Rennie dismissed the appeal and established two critical principles34. First, citing Kam-Press, the FCA rejected the taxpayer's contention that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are mere non-binding guidance or that applied sciences follow an "engineering method" distinct from the scientific method (noting also that trying to introduce an article in a book of authorities on appeal was an impermissible attempt to introduce trial evidence through the back door)34. Second, the FCA upheld the Tax Court's refusal to qualify the taxpayer's proposed external expert witness because: (a) the report failed to comply with the Tax Court Rules and Experts' Code of Conduct; (b) the taxpayer wrote 65% of the proposed expert's report, destroying impartiality and independence and turning the report into advocacy; (c) the report improperly offered a legal opinion on whether the expenditures qualified under the Income Tax Act; and (d) it failed the gatekeeper balancing stage34.

Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108 (TCC): Canafric Inc., a food manufacturer producing custom frozen pies for retail clients (Costco, Loblaws, Mortimer), appealed the CRA's disallowance of SR&ED projects across the 2013 to 2016 taxation years (totalling $343,449 in denied expenditures and $60,963 in denied ITCs, excluding undisclosed 2014 amounts)28. The projects sought to achieve longer shelf life (including a 21-day shelf life without preservatives), reduce salt and fat, increase protein, maintain product and crust integrity after freezing, use real potatoes and antibiotic-free or halal meat, and reduce cooking times28. The Tax Court ruled in favour of Canafric and allowed the claims on three grounds28: (1) Systematic Analysis vs. Trial and Error: Rejecting the CRA's argument that Canafric used mere trial and error, the Court found that Canafric translated client targets into testable recipe hypotheses, analyzed why recipes failed, and adjusted formulations systematically28; (2) Unsuccessful Formulations Constitute Technological Advancement: Even where Canafric failed to meet all client targets, systematically eliminating options advanced technological understanding under Paragraph 248(1)(c)28; and (3) Credible Oral Testimony Bridging Documentary Gaps: Applying RIS-Christie, the Court held that the impressive, factually based, and credible oral testimony of Canafric's CEO (Mr. Pandya) at trial filled in gaps in the documentary record where the CRA had failed to address the appellant's evidence28.
